result.summary: Medea and Jason part after exchanging promises and tales of their homelands, and Jason tells his comrades of her plan. After a night rite to Hecate, he uses Medea's charm to yoke the fire-breathing bulls, plough the field and sow the dragon's teeth. He then defeats the earthborn warriors by throwing a boulder among them, and Aeetes leaves in grief.

scenes.title: Medea and Jason's farewell
scenes.summary: Medea asks about his home, and Jason tells of Haemonia and Ariadne. They pledge to remember each other and part at the day's end.
scenes.stakes: Medea risks her family and homeland for a stranger who may forget her; Jason needs her help to survive.

scenes.title: Medea returns to the palace
scenes.summary: Medea drives home in a daze, and Chalciope questions her in vain. She sits grieving over what she has done.
scenes.stakes: Medea fears the consequences of betraying her father.

scenes.title: Jason reports to the Argonauts
scenes.summary: Jason tells the heroes of Medea's counsel and shows the charm. Idas sulks, and at dawn Telamon and Aethalides go to ask Aeetes for the seed.

scenes.title: The dragon's teeth of Cadmus
scenes.summary: Aeetes hands over the teeth, whose history is told: Cadmus slew the dragon at Thebes, Athena gave half the teeth to Aeetes, and Cadmus sowed the rest.

scenes.title: Jason's rite to Hecate
scenes.summary: At night Jason bathes, sacrifices a ewe and calls on Hecate Brimo, who appears with serpents, torches and hounds. Frightened, he returns to his comrades.
scenes.stakes: Jason needs the goddess's aid to survive the contest and risks her terrifying wrath.

place.name: Meadow by the sacred river, Colchis

scenes.title: Arming for the contest
scenes.summary: Aeetes arrives in his chariot. Jason charms his weapons and the heroes sail to the plain of Ares.
scenes.stakes: Jason's life depends on the charm's protection.

scenes.title: Jason yokes the bulls
scenes.summary: Jason withstands the fire-breathing bulls, forces them down, yokes them with the help of the Tyndaridae, and ploughs and sows the field.
scenes.stakes: Jason faces death by flame and bronze hooves, with only Medea's charm to protect him.

scenes.title: The earthborn harvest
scenes.summary: Armed warriors spring up, and Jason's boulder makes them kill one another. He cuts down the rest, and Aeetes returns grieving to plot against the heroes.
scenes.stakes: Jason risks being overwhelmed by a whole army of earthborn warriors.

notable_quotes.reason: Medea's plea to be remembered captures her fear of abandonment.
The narrator foreshadows Medea's fate in Hellas.

analysis.text: Love and betrayal intertwine: Medea's devotion to Jason costs her family and home, and the poet hints at tragedy ahead.
The tale of Cadmus's dragon teeth ties the Colchian myth to Greek Theban legend, in learned Hellenistic style.

legacy.text: The sown dragon's teeth that become warriors gave later literature the image of 'sowing dragon's teeth', meaning causing future strife.
The film Jason and the Argonauts (1963) features warriors rising from sown teeth, with Ray Harryhausen's skeleton fight.

fun_facts.text: The Argonautica was written by Apollonius of Rhodes in the 3rd century BC and is the only surviving Hellenistic epic.

language_notes.text: Orchomenus is a wealthy Boeotian city founded by Minyas, ancestor of many Argonauts; the Aeaean isle is Circe's island, which Medea knows as kin.
Ariadne, Minos' daughter, helped Theseus escape the Labyrinth; Jason had mentioned her earlier. Pasiphae, her mother, was sister of Aeetes, so Medea is her cousin.
Ioleus (also spelled Iolcus) is Jason's city in Haemonia, later called Thessaly; Orchomenus lay near Thebes, home of the Cadmeians.
Jason wishes Aeetes might favour them as Minos favoured Theseus, a hopeful and somewhat naive comparison.
"I ween" means "I think" or "I suppose"; "guest-love" is the bond of friendship and loyalty between host and guest.
The "messenger-bird" is a bird carrying news or omen; Medea wishes either word of his forgetting her or a storm that carries her to him.
Medea would later come to Iolcus and bring about the death of Pelias, who had sent Jason on this quest.
Her soul 'soared amid the clouds' means her mind was far away, wholly absorbed in thoughts of Jason; she is oblivious to those around her.
'Biting down his wrath' means swallowing his anger in silence; Idas resents relying on Medea's help rather than on fighting.
'Aonian' means Boeotian, the region around Thebes; 'Ogygian' is an old poetic epithet for Thebes, from the legendary king Ogygus.
Cadmus came from Phoenicia searching for his sister Europa, who had been carried off by Zeus; he then founded Thebes.
Apollo's oracle told Cadmus to follow a heifer and found a city where it lay down; this place became Thebes.
'Tritonian goddess' is Athena, so called from the river or lake Triton, one of her cult titles.
Sown dragon's teeth sprang up as armed men who killed one another; the survivors became the Thebans' ancestors, the Spartoi.
Heliee is the Greek name for the Great Bear constellation, used by sailors for navigation. Its setting marks the deep of night.
Hypsipyle, queen of Lemnos, bore Jason's children after the Argonauts stayed there earlier in the voyage. The robe is her parting gift.
Libations are liquids, here mixed offerings such as milk and honey, poured out to a deity. A cubit is roughly the length of a forearm.
"Hounds of hell" are the spectral dogs that attend Hecate as a goddess of the underworld and of night magic.
Phlegraean Mimas was one of the Giants who fought the gods at Phlegra. Aeetes, son of the Sun, claims help from Ares in that war.
Heracles was left behind in Mysia earlier in the voyage, so the Argonauts lack their strongest fighter.
The places listed are sites sacred to Poseidon, such as the Isthmus of Corinth and Taenarus, where he was worshipped with games and shrines.
The comparison refers to funeral games, a Greek custom of racing in honour of a dead king, with a turning-post marking the course.
Adamant is a legendary unbreakable metal, here used for the plough; it signals the equipment is divine, not ordinary iron.
Steading means a farmstead or dwelling place; here it is the bulls' underground stable.
The 'foot of bronze' refers to the bull's bronze hoof; Jason kicks its leg to buckle it.
The sentence is awkward: the Tyndaridae (Castor and Polydeuces) handed Jason the yoke, as had long been arranged beforehand, presumably by Jason's plan.
A Pelasgian goad is an ox-prod from the Pelasgians, the early inhabitants of Greece; Jason uses his spear like a ploughman's goad.
A plough-gate is a measure of land, the area a plough could work; the field is four of these.
The plot of Ares is the field sown with dragon's teeth, sacred to the war god. Olympus is the mountain home of the gods.
A quoit is a heavy throwing disc. Enyalius is a war-god title attached to Ares, here used as an epithet.
The counsels of Medea refer to her earlier advice: throw a boulder among the earthborn men so they turn on each other.
"Earth their mother" recalls that these warriors were born from the soil, so they fall back into the earth that bore them.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose"; the narrator interjects a personal comment.

context_notes.text: Love is Eros, who has been made to strike Jason and Medea at Hera's urging.
Prometheus, the Titan who gave fire to humans, is here made father of Deucalion, the Greek flood survivor who repopulated the earth.
Hera favours Jason and protects the Argonauts; she wants Pelias punished for neglecting her honours.
Medea drives a mule-drawn chariot; mules were common draught animals, and a royal princess might drive herself.
Chalciope is Medea's sister, mother of sons by Phrixus, who are among the Argonauts' allies; hence her anxiety.
Telamon was a famed hero, father of Ajax; Aethalides, a son of Hermes, served as herald of the Argonauts.
Hecate was a goddess of night, witchcraft and the underworld; Brimo ("the angry one") is her epithet. Medea has told Jason to sacrifice to her.
Phaethon here is Aeetes' charioteer, not the famous son of the Sun who crashed his father's chariot.
Idas, son of Aphareus, is a proud and violent Argonaut, known for his quick temper.
The maiden is Medea, who gave Jason a charmed ointment making him immune to fire and weapons.
Aeetes is king of Colchis, who set this impossible task hoping Jason would die.
The sons of Tyndareus are Castor and Polydeuces (Pollux), Argonauts and brothers of Helen, who stand by Jason during the trial.
The teeth are dragon's teeth, which will grow into armed earthborn warriors once sown.
The warriors grow from dragon's teeth Jason sowed, as Aeetes required in the ordeal he set for Jason to win the Golden Fleece.
Aeetes, king of Colchis, had set the ordeal expecting Jason to fail, so his defeat leads him to scheme against the Argonauts.

literary_notes.text: Love is presented as a figure who steals over Jason, making his feeling seem an external, overwhelming force.
Medea shows her insight and insecurity by contrasting her harsh father with Minos and doubting she can match Ariadne.
Medea's wish to appear unexpectedly as a reproachful guest anticipates her later actual arrival in Iolcus under very different circumstances.
The narrator warns that Medea will soon leave for Hellas, hinting at the tragic future that follows.
Her soul flying among the clouds figures her love-struck distraction as physical flight, explaining why she ignores everyone.
Medea's posture and tears show remorse and inner conflict, revealing her as a young girl troubled by betraying her father.
Aeetes confidently believes Jason will fail, but the reader knows Medea's charm gives Jason a chance to succeed.
Comparing Jason to a stealthy thief stresses the secrecy and illicit quality of his night-time magic rite.
Serpents, torches and howling hounds create a vivid, terrifying picture of the goddess's arrival.
Aeetes' golden helmet is likened to the rising sun, fitting for the Sun's son and suggesting his dazzling power.
The long comparison to Poseidon's progress through his sacred places lends Aeetes divine grandeur.
The eager warhorse conveys Jason's restless, joyful energy once the charm fills him with strength.
Jason's flashing leaps are compared to lightning from storm clouds, showing his brilliance and menace.
Jason's steadiness is likened to a rock reef enduring waves, conveying immovability against the bulls' rush.
The bulls' flaming breath is compared at length to a furnace and its bellows, adding craftsman's detail and rising intensity.
Jason is compared to an ordinary ploughman, making the supernatural labour seem humble and ironic in scale.
The bulls' breath is compared to storm winds that make sailors furl sails, linking the field to the sea.
Jason's backward glances anticipate the earthborn warriors who will spring from the teeth.
Jason's rising fury is compared to a boar whetting its tusks, showing his fierce readiness before the fight.
The armed men gleaming from the soil are likened to stars appearing after clouds clear, a beautiful image for a deadly sight.
Jason is compared to a shooting star, an omen to men, suggesting his rapid, striking and fateful attack.
Jason's slaughter is likened to a farmer reaping unripe grain, which turns the earthborn men into a literal crop.
Aeetes' grief is compared to a farmer's ruined orchard, giving the cruel king a moment of human sympathy.
